newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Mandela confident of Southeast Asian investment.
newsitem.headline: Mandela confident of Southeast Asian investment.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Thursday he was confident Southeast Asia would be eager to trade and invest in Africa as communication between the two continents improved.

"With the opening up of communication between Africa and this region, I have not the slightest doubt that they will grasp at the opportunity to trade and invest in Africa," Mandela told a news conference.

He cited Malaysia as one of the region's leading investors in Africa and pointed to Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's visit to four southern African countries as an indication of closer ties between the regions.

Mandela, who is due to leave for Malaysia later on Thursday on the last leg of a four-nation Asian tour, said South Africa and Singapore had signed agreements covering taxation, air travel, technical assistance and were finalising a pact to protect investments.
He said South Africa could offer the region expertise in a number of areas such as mining and added that the country aimed to exploit its strategic location between South America and Asia.
"One of our priorities is to expand our export base because it is a little bit narrow. And to ensure that our exports to the world exceed our imports," Mandela said.

On the role of South Africa's trade unions, Mandela said they had contributed to the country's democratic transformation but continued to grapple with problems such as wage disparities between workers of different races.
He said the South African government would display the same patience and openness to dialogue it had shown the apartheid regime in its dealings with the trade unions.

On the use of international economic pressure to protest against human rights abuses in Burma, Mandela said South Africa would be willing to play a part in any coordinated action by the United Nations or the Commonwealth of Nations.
"We are part of the international community and we resist acting unilaterally, independently of the structures that exist," he said.
The South African leader said his country would abide by its promise to maintain economic relations with Taiwan at the highest level after it terminates diplomatic ties at the end of this year.
"Taiwan has known that the moment would come when we would fall in line with the decision of the United Nations, of which we are members," Mandela said.
